title: 6 Mindsets of Excellent Educators
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart argues that teacher excellence comes from shared mindsets rather than personality or teaching style. He identifies six: a 'never finished' professional dissatisfaction paired with personal satisfaction at day's end; a deliberate work-life balance; a long-term vision of the career, likened to ultra-runners who walk the hills; reverence for the instructional minute; an aggressive, productive relationship with failure made possible by detaching self-worth from performance; and a commitment to being on the same team as colleagues. He contrasts the balance he describes with the success-at-all-costs teachers portrayed in films. He argues that whole-system change comes from groups of teachers, not individuals, so excellent educators resist gossip and division even when policies pit them against each other. He closes by framing teaching as a refining fire that both improves the work and improves the teacher.
points: Stuart's central claim is that excellent teachers share mindsets, not personalities or styles.
The 'never finished' mindset pairs professional dissatisfaction with personal satisfaction, which fuels improvement without burnout.
Excellent teachers protect work-life balance and take a long-term view of the career, rejecting the self-sacrificing teacher of the movies.
Failure is treated as free, ongoing professional schooling, which is possible only when self-worth is detached from work performance.
Because groups, not individuals, change systems, excellent teachers resist gossip and praise colleagues behind their backs while speaking hard truths face-to-face.
quotes: Each of them are excellent teachers, and I'd argue that their excellence is something separate from personality or teaching style.

The thing about great teachers is that they are professionally dissatisfied with their shortcomings, their weaknesses, their mistakes, their inability to overcome present obstacles. And yet, because they believe that they can change and improve (in short, they have Carol Dweck's famous growth mindset), this dissatisfaction acts as a pleasant fuel that drives them to exert themselves toward improvement with every working hour.

Great teachers are just like these ultra-runners. They realize that a teaching career is a long path, and greatest are the rewards for those who stick to the work until they've put in enough deliberate practice to cross into excellence.

Their students are engaged in some form of thinking, reading, writing, or speaking from bell-to-bell; when kids are listening to the teacher, it's for a focused, organized message or lesson — not an endless, time-consuming string of self-indulgent anecdotes.

This intimacy with failure is only possible because these teachers have intentionally sought to detach their sense of self-worth from how well they're performing at work. Doing this is, as they say, “an inside job,” but it's critical if one wants to be able to analyze one's practice as objectively as possible.

They seek to rid themselves of self-righteousness or arrogance because they know, either instinctively or because the research supports it, that individual teachers do not create whole system change — groups of teachers do.
I'll end with the first mindset: remember that we're never finished working on improving as teachers, and we're never finished letting our work as teachers improve us. This work is a refining fire.
